newsitem.title: EGYPT: Israel, PLO trade jabs on Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO trade jabs on Hebron.

text.p: Israel and the PLO sniped at each other as they adjourned talks on Friday without agreeing on a long-delayed Israeli redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron.
Palestinians blamed Israel for a setback in negotiations.
Israel, in response to the Palestinian charge, accused the PLO of spreading "disinformation".
Going into the talks at Israel's Eilat Red Sea resort, Palestinians had thought a deal on Hebron, where 400 Jewish settlers live amid 100,000 Palestinians, was in sight.
Palestinians and Arab states regard the Hebron redeployment as a litmus test of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's intentions regarding the peace process.
But negotiators left Eilat before dawn on Friday saying no deal had yet been struck. The sides later met for two hours in the Egyptian vacation spot of Taba just across the border.

"Unfortunately, up to this moment I don't think the Israeli government has given the negotiators a green light to go ahead with the implementation," chief Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told CNN television after Friday's talks.

Negotiator Hassan Asfour said the two sides agreed to resume talks on Monday alternating between Eilat and Taba on the Egyptian side of the border. He said subcommittees would meet during the weekend.
Israeli officials denied Palestinian reports of disputes between political and military representatives on the Israeli delegation and said progress had been reached during the last week of talks.

"We are making progress in the negotiations...I think that in the last week, in the last few days, some progress was made, some gaps were closed between the sides. I hope this trend continues next week," Israeli cabinet secretary Danny Naveh told Israel Television.
Israeli negotiating team head Dan Shomron said a solution was "very close" but he did not elaborate.

Palestinian officials had said Israel was no longer insisting on a buffer zone to divide Israeli and PLO forces in Hebron or on the right of "hot pursuit", allowing Israel to chase wanted Palestinians in areas coming under PLO control.

But Israeli media, quoting sources on the Israeli team, on Friday said that far from Israel dropping the demands, the sides were working on a compromise in which a joint PLO-Israeli force would carry out hot pursuit and patrol buffer areas.
Israel's Haaretz daily, quoting a senior Israeli source, said Netanyahu approved the proposal. Asfour denied the reports.
Israel's previous government in September 1995 signed a deal with the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) to expand Palestinian self-rule in the West Bank.
Under the deal, Israel was to redeploy from seven West Bank towns including Hebron. It was also to begin pulling back from rural West Bank areas by September 1996.

Six towns were handed over to the PLO last year but the partial pullback from Hebron, due to have occurred in March, was delayed after Islamic suicide attacks in February and March killed 59 people in Israel.
Netanyahu, elected in May, put the deal on hold, saying changes were needed to enhance security for Jewish settlers but Palestinians refuse to reopen the agreement.
